edits.old: Finite divisors on a fixed manifold now have an exact Gauduchon feasibility threshold and a residual variational volume. Divisorial currents on each modification also have finite Gauduchon mass. These facts are compatible with the lack of any uniform upper Monge--Amp\`ere mass bound on the original manifold.
edits.new: Finite divisors on a fixed manifold now have an exact Gauduchon feasibility threshold and a residual variational volume. If the residual background has a smooth positive representative and the prescribed probability measure is smooth and strictly positive, \cref{thm:divisorial-residual-equation} gives a smooth residual solution. Every threshold subsolution whose divisorial coefficients dominate the prescribed ones differs from it by a constant; no bounded-remainder assumption is needed. A solution in the prescribed ordinary type therefore has the same scalar and a smooth remainder. Divisorial currents on each modification also have finite Gauduchon mass. These facts are compatible with the lack of any uniform upper Monge--Amp\`ere mass bound on the original manifold.

edits.old:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:divisorial-residual-equation}
Suppose $\beta_D$ admits a smooth positive representative. There is a $\theta$-plurisubharmonic potential $u=\sigma_D+v$, with $v$ smooth, satisfying
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u)
           =\mathcal V_\mu(\theta;D)\,\mu.
\]
The normalized smooth remainder and the positive scalar are unique among such smooth-remainder solutions. More generally, if a solution in the ordinary singularity type of $\sigma_D$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u)=c\mu$, then its scalar must equal $\mathcal V_\mu(\theta;D)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Solve the smooth equation in $\beta_D$:
\[
 \Omega=\beta_D+\ddc v>0,
 \qquad \Omega^n=c\mu,
 \qquad c=\mathcal V_\mu(\beta_D),
\]
using \cref{thm:gaud-volume-dual-formula}. Then $\theta+\ddc(\sigma_D+v)=[D]+\Omega$ is positive. On the complement of the divisor its non-pluripolar measure is $\Omega^n$. Both this smooth measure and the extended product give zero mass to the divisor, so the identity holds globally. The smooth uniqueness theorem in the residual background proves uniqueness of $v$ after an additive normalization and uniqueness of its scalar in this class.

For the last assertion write $u=\sigma_D+w$ in $L^1$, with $w$ bounded. Its divisorial coefficients along $D_j$ are $a_j$. The same divisorial removal used in \cref{prop:divisorial-gaud-feasibility} gives
$\beta_D+\ddc w=\theta+\ddc u-[D]\geq0$.
Thus $w$ has a bounded $\beta_D$-plurisubharmonic representative. Both products below give the divisor zero mass, and their equality off it follows by locality. Hence
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u)=(\beta_D+\ddc w)^n.
\]
Choose a smooth $v_0$ with $\Omega_0=\beta_D+\ddc v_0>0$. The functions $w-v_0$ and $v-v_0$ are bounded $\Omega_0$-plurisubharmonic. If their positive scalars differed, the measure of the smaller-scalar potential would be bounded by a constant strictly smaller than one times the measure of the other. Apply \cref{thm:bounded-strict-domination} after every constant translation of the latter potential. It would force the former to dominate arbitrarily large translates, which is impossible. The case $c=0$ is excluded by non-collapse of bounded potentials in a Hermitian background. Thus the scalar is the displayed one. This last argument does not assert uniqueness of the bounded remainder.
\end{proof}

edits.new:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:divisorial-residual-equation}
Suppose $\beta_D$ admits a smooth positive representative, and put $c=\mathcal V_\mu(\theta;D)$. There is a $\theta$-plurisubharmonic potential $u_0=\sigma_D+v$, with $v$ smooth, satisfying
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u_0)=c\mu.
\]
Every $u\in\PSH(X,\theta)$ such that
\[
 \nu(u,D_j)\geq a_j\quad(1\leq j\leq N),\qquad
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u)\geq c\mu
\]
is a constant translate of $u_0$. In particular, a solution in the ordinary singularity type of $\sigma_D$ has scalar $c$, has a smooth remainder, and is unique up to constants.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The smooth equation and \cref{thm:gaud-volume-dual-formula} give
\[
 \Omega=\beta_D+\ddc v>0,\qquad \Omega^n=c\mu.
\]
Then $\theta+\ddc(\sigma_D+v)=[D]+\Omega\geq0$. Off $D$ its extended measure is $\Omega^n$, and both measures give $D$ zero mass. This proves existence.

For a potential $u$ satisfying the displayed inequalities, divisorial removal as in \cref{prop:divisorial-gaud-feasibility} makes
\[
 w=u-\sigma_D-v\in\PSH(X,\Omega),\qquad
 \Omega+\ddc w=\theta+\ddc u-[D]\geq0.
\]
The difference is first taken in $L^1$ and then with its canonical representative. On $X\setminus D$ the two currents have smooth changes of local potential decomposition, so their extended measures agree there. Both measures vanish on $D$. Hence
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\Omega(w)
       =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u)\geq c\mu.
\]
Use $\mathrm{d}V=\mu$. The zero potential solves the smooth equation in background $\Omega$, so $b_\Omega(1)=c$ by \cref{prop:individual-normalizer-lp}. For $n\geq2$, its Gauduchon representative gives a smooth strictly positive dual maximizer. By \cref{cor:smooth-dual-exact-equation}, all threshold subsolutions differ by constants; comparing $w$ with zero shows that $w$ is constant. For $n=1$, the positive current $\Omega+\ddc w$ dominates its extended measure, hence dominates $c\mu=\Omega$. Its total mass is $\int_X\Omega=c$ by Stokes. Thus $\ddc w=0$, and $w$ is again constant.

Finally, if $u$ lies in the ordinary type of $\sigma_D$ and solves an equation with scalar $c'\geq0$, the same reduction gives a bounded $w$ with $\mathrm{MA}_\Omega(w)=c'\mu$. If $c'\ne c$, the smaller of these two measures is at most a constant strictly less than one times the larger. Applying \cref{thm:bounded-strict-domination} after every constant translation of the larger-measure potential is impossible. Therefore $c'=c$, and the rigidity just proved gives $u=u_0+\mathrm{constant}$.
\end{proof}
